description:
YACHASKA — Stories Beyond the Stars

Hi! I’m Jokabel, a software engineering technician studying data science. I’m building YACHASKA, a creative project blending science, storytelling, art, and interactive web development to bring forgotten NASA machines on the Moon and Mars back into the spotlight.

I welcome developers, writers, artists, designers, and space enthusiasts who want to create, learn, and explore together. No expertise required—just curiosity, commitment, and a passion for the idea. Join YACHASKA and help bring these stories to life!
summary:
We developed YACHASKA, an interactive, offline-first web storybook that turns the hardware NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space into storytellers for children in the Andes and the Amazon, in their own languages. Inspired by the Ayacucho retablo, a traditional Andean art form from Peru, a painted box opens into space: the Apollo 17 Lunar Rover, the Apollo 11 laser retroreflector, the Voyager Golden Record, Spirit and Ingenuity narrate their missions in first person. Across 8 chapters and 56 scenes, each scene pairs narrated text with a verified NASA fact and its source, plus an "Andean bridge" linking the science to ancestral knowledge.

It answers the challenge by showing that discarded space equipment is not junk but the heritage of humanity. More than 4.4 million people in Peru learned to speak in Quechua, Aymara, Asháninka, Awajún or Shipibo-Konibo (INEI, 2017 Census), yet space science almost never reaches them in those languages. YACHASKA works in seven languages, runs on low-end phones, works offline after the first visit, and has no ads or tracking. Quechua already travels beyond the solar system on the Voyager Golden Record. YACHASKA brings that story home, because what is told in your language is never forgotten.
details:
WHAT DOES IT DO?

YACHASKA is a narrative learning platform about space heritage for children aged 8–14 and their teachers in rural Andean and Amazonian communities of Peru.

  1. It turns five pieces of NASA hardware into characters that tell their own missions in first person: the Apollo 17 Lunar Roving Vehicle, the Apollo 11 laser retroreflector, the Voyager Golden Record, the Spirit rover and the Ingenuity helicopter.
  2. It teaches with verified data: each of the 56 scenes includes a NASA fact with a direct link to its source.
  3. It connects space science to local knowledge through an "Andean bridge" in each scene: the laser that bounces off the Moon is a chasqui runner on the Qhapaq Ñan, Ingenuity is a q'inti hummingbird flying in thin air, and the data it stores is its own quipu.
  4. It speaks 7 languages, switchable mid-story: Spanish and English (complete), Quechua (complete, under native-speaker review), and Aymara, Asháninka, Awajún and Shipibo-Konibo (drafts, clearly labeled in the app).
  5. It is listen-first: 168 narration files (56 scenes in Spanish, English and Quechua) let children who do not yet read fluently follow the whole story by ear.
  6. It works offline after the first visit, so it can be used in schools with weak or no internet.
  7. It supports teachers with a 1969–2026 timeline, a catalogue of "the ones who stayed", a table of Indigenous languages with speaker figures, a full sources section and a CSV export of the script for translators.

HOW DOES IT WORK?

  1. NASA data research: we documented five objects left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space using NASA Science, NSSDCA, JPL and the NASA History Office, plus NASA public-domain images.
  2. Fact verification: every figure was checked against its NASA source, and each scene keeps a direct link to it.
  3. Story design: each scene has three layers: a first-person text, a NASA fact and an Andean bridge (8 chapters, 56 scenes, plus a prologue and an epilogue).
  4. Cultural interface: the design is inspired by the Ayacucho retablo, a traditional Andean art form from Peru: a painted wooden box that tells stories floor by floor. The child taps the golden latch, the doors open, and each floor is a chapter.
  5. Multilingual narration: Spanish and English are narrated with neural voices; Quechua uses an open Ayacucho Quechua voice model; the other Indigenous-language drafts are exported to a CSV sheet for native-speaker review.
  6. Offline-first delivery: a static web app with a service worker stores the page and the audio of the chosen language (about 6 MB) on the phone.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

  1. Educational: brings NASA missions, planetary science and space heritage to children who rarely have access to them, with every claim traceable to a NASA source.
  2. Cultural and linguistic: treats Indigenous languages and Andean knowledge as ways of understanding the universe, and keeps endangered languages alive in a scientific context. More than 4.4 million people in Peru speak Quechua, Aymara, Asháninka, Awajún or Shipibo-Konibo as their mother tongue (INEI, 2017 Census).
  3. Social: free, no account, no ads, no cookies, no tracking; works on low-end phones without internet.
  4. Heritage awareness: helps a new generation see the objects on the Moon and Mars as heritage to be protected.
  5. Next steps: pilot with teachers in schools in Huanta and other districts of Ayacucho; native speakers review and record the Indigenous-language versions; new chapters about Artemis and lunar heritage protection.

HOW IS IT CREATIVE?

The machines are the narrators, and the interface is inspired by a real Andean storytelling craft, the Ayacucho retablo. Science and ancestral knowledge sit side by side in every scene. The project starts from a real link between NASA and the Andes: a Quechua greeting already travels beyond the solar system on the Voyager Golden Record.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

  1. Low connectivity: offline mode.
  2. Low-end phones: light static files, about 2 MB without audio.
  3. Children who do not read fluently: narration first.
  4. Linguistic accuracy: Indigenous-language versions are labeled as drafts until native speakers validate them.
  5. Privacy: no personal data; children appear only as illustrations.
  6. Accessibility: keyboard navigation, reduced motion, large touch targets, night and day themes.
  7. Scientific validity: every fact is linked to its NASA source.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE

  1. Languages: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (vanilla, no framework), Python.
  2. Web: IntersectionObserver scrollytelling, SVG illustrations drawn in code, WebP images, Service Worker API, Cache Storage, Web Speech API.
  3. Narration: edge-tts (Microsoft neural voices) for Spanish and English; Meta MMS-TTS facebook/mms-tts-quy for Ayacucho Quechua.
  4. Development: Visual Studio Code, Google Antigravity IDE, Git, GitHub.
  5. Hosting: Vercel (https://yachaska.vercel.app); source code at https://github.com/Juan-Ayme/yachaska.
  6. Demo video: ElevenLabs (voice-over), FFmpeg (editing), NASA public-domain photos.
  7. Hardware: laptops for development; Android and iOS phones for testing.

USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (DISCLOSURE)

  1. Code: Claude (Anthropic) assisted with code generation and debugging; Google Antigravity IDE with Gemini assisted with generating and organizing image assets. AI-assisted code is acknowledged in the repository README.
  2. Text: Claude assisted in drafting the Spanish and English story text and this documentation, and produced first drafts of the Quechua, Aymara, Asháninka, Awajún and Shipibo-Konibo versions. The app labels these as AI-assisted drafts pending native-speaker review.
  3. Images: the storybook illustrations and retablo-inspired assets (doors, crest, flowers, buttons, language banners, icons) were generated with Google Gemini image generation; some SVG illustrations were drawn in code with Claude. Images on the project page and in the demo carry a visible "AI-assisted" mark.
  4. Audio: the app narration uses synthetic voices (Microsoft neural voices via edge-tts for Spanish and English; Meta MMS-TTS for Quechua). The demo video voice-over was generated with ElevenLabs (Eleven v4, "Ladypatty – Warm Latin voice"). This is stated in the app's "AI" section, in the video description and in the video file metadata.
  5. Human work: the team chose the challenge and created the concept, the retablo-inspired frame, the characters, the Andean bridges and the story structure. They also directed the art and checked every NASA fact against its source.
  6. NASA branding: no NASA logos, insignia, flags or mission identifiers were used or modified in any AI-generated content.
